set.hook: Stone Town's main food market since 1904: spice by the scoop, fish on slabs, fruit and grain.
set.why: The tin-roofed hall on Market Street was opened in August 1904 for Sultan Ali bin Hamud, designed by the British architect J.H. set.hook: Unguja's oldest lighthouse, a white stone tower lit in 1926 at the island's northern point.
set.why: Ras Nungwi, which old charts call Hog Point, is the northern tip of Unguja, and a light has marked it since the 1880s. The tower there now is a white square stone tower in three stages, built in 1926: 14 metres tall with a focal height of 18 metres, and its white flash reaches 13 nautical miles. The Zanzibar Ports Corporation still runs it as a working light, so you see it from outside only.

set.hook: A west-facing beach on Unguja where the sea stays close at low tide, so you can swim most of the day.
set.why: Along most of Zanzibar's east and south-east coast the sea goes out a long way at low tide and you plan swims around the tide table. Kendwa, on the north-west coast, shelves quickly, so the water is deep enough to swim in for most of the day whatever the tide is doing. It also faces west, so you can stay in the water until the sun goes down.

set.hook: A private atoll off Unguja's north-east coast, ringed by a marine conservation area you reach by boat.
set.why: The island is private, run as an &Beyond lodge, and day boats cannot land, so the trip is entirely about the water around it, which is a protected marine area with its own entry fee. After the February 2024 global bleaching hit the reef, &Beyond and Wild Impact began fixing hexagonal steel 'reef stars', built by people from nearby villages, onto the coral rubble and planting them with nursery-grown fragments.

set.hook: A submerged mountain in the Pemba Channel north of Nungwi, an advanced drift dive in strong current.
set.why: Leven Bank is a seamount out in the Pemba Channel whose top sits about fourteen metres down, and divers with the right qualifications go to around fifty. The current across it is strong enough that the north-tip centres pick the day by conditions, not by the calendar, and take only experienced divers. Those who go come back describing large groupers, moray eels, tuna and barracuda, and sometimes rays or dolphins.

set.hook: The cathedral on the site of Zanzibar's last open slave market, with holding chambers and a memorial.
set.why: Sultan Barghash closed the public slave market under British pressure in 1873, and missionaries built Christ Church on the same ground, opening it in 1879. A heritage centre at the gate, opened in 2016, tells the trade's story before you reach the cramped holding chambers. Outside, five figures by the Swedish artist Clara Sörnäs, installed in 1998, stand in a pit, chained at the neck.
